subject: spatial covariates at integration points: INLA vs inlabru

messages.author: e1bb761489868f5d
messages.subject: spatial covariates at integration points: INLA vs inlabru
parts:
Hi all,

This is more of a question regarding model fitting rather than an issue I have with my code. I am trying to build a point process model that includes several of continuous covariates along with a spde component. At first I started creating these models using the R-INLA package but have recently transition to the inlabru package due to it ease with model development and prediction. 

However, now I am confused how adding spatial covariates between the packages differ between the packages, particularly at the integration points? From Krainski et al. (2019), their example of adding spatial covariates to a LGCP model indicates that the "For model fitting, we must know the value of the covariate at the location points and integration points" for which they that explicitly in their example. The inlabru example of adding in continuous spatial covariates does not show how the covariates values are associated with the integration points. The inlabru example only shows extracting the continuous spatial covariates at the locations (through the function f.elev) but not at the integration points. This makes me curious what is inlabru doing differently? I am familiar with the Simpson et al. (2013) method and point process models (using a glm framework for example) where the quadratures are also given values of the spatial covariate. I saw from this thread that inlabru does not apply the Simpson method but rather approximates the LGCP a bit differently (and more accurately!). Would it be possible to explain what inlabru is doing regarding spatial covariates at the integration points (I am an ecologist, so a more intuitive explanation may better help my understanding). Any help would be greatly appreciated!

Thanks,
Nima

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] spatial covariates at integration points: INLA vs inlabru
parts:
Hi,

in the continuous spatial covariates vignette, the initial version was
confusing on this point; the current version is a bit better, but
still not ideal; if you look at the "vegetation" covariate instead it
should be clearer; that that covariate takes discrete values is not
relevant to how it's accessed; the f.eval() could be used for either
discrete or continuous covariates; the "continuous" aspect is that
_space_ is treated as continuous. Instead of
elev(f.elev(coordinates(.data.)), model = "linear")
use
elev(gcov$elevation, model = "linear")

This also preserves any crs information, so that you don't
accidentally end up evaluating the covariate in the wrong place.

The automated covariate elevation calls the eval_spatial() function,
which is essentially an encapsulation of the old "f.covar()" function
examples. We still present the "f.covar()" approach in the vignette
to show how to do it if the eval_spatial() method for some reason
doesn't do what's needed in any particular special case.

When it comes to the Simpson et al (2013) paper, inlabry _does_ apply
that method, and it's rather several other examples that incorrectly
describe what that method is. The Simpson et al method uses the
lambda(s) values at each observed point for the \sum_i
log(lambda(y_i)) part of the likelihood, and the values of lambda(s)
at the integration points for the integral approximation part.
Methods that use aggregated counts at each vertex are different, and
_not_ what we developed in Simpson et al.

Finn

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] spatial covariates at integration points: INLA vs inlabru
parts:
...and to further explain what inlabru is doing; When you supply
observed points, domain, and samplers information to inlabru, it
constructs the integration scheme internally (by calling
fmesher::fm_int()).
It then evaluates the component inputs, using the observed point
locations and integration points. When the input is a spatial grid
object, it calls eval_spatial() for all those locations to obtain the
covariate values.

Finn

parts:
Hi Finn,

Thank you so much this explanation. It really helps! So if I am understanding this correctly, the covariates (continuous or categorial) need to be provided as some sort of gridded object like a SpatialPixelsDataFrame, raster layer, etc. and not extracting the covariate at the locations before hand (for example using the f.covar function and then creating the model like so.....

ecomp <- coordinates ~ elev + mySmooth(coordinates, model = matern) + Intercept(1)
...where elev is the covariate values at each location of what you are studying).

What if, lets say, the locations for what you are trying to model are matched with monthly or seasonal environmental data (i.e. not static like elevation). I assume then this framework, where we are using a single gridded object, would not work and I would need to construct the integration scheme for the temporal scale at which the locations are at (i.e. construct an integration scheme at the month/seasonal scale and match them with the month / seasonal environmental data). This seems like I would need to construct a spatiotemporal LGCP model following the methods here. However, how would I make sure that the integration points for each month or season is matched with the concurrent environmental data?

Hopefully this all makes sense! Again, thanks for your help!

-Nima
